Losing a Single “Molecular Brake” Gene Triggers Brain Overgrowth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene.
  • Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.
  • Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene. The single-cell lineage-tracing study reveals that individual neural progenitors lacking Pten generate 25% more neurons alongside an excess of enlarged astrocytes, and reroute glial cell production through the MAPK pathway, offering a potential upcoming target for drug-resistant brain tumors.

Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.

Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.

Acting as a vital molecular brake during this process is the Pten gene, which restrains cell division and keeps tissue growth balanced.

When mutations disable PTEN, that biological brake fails. Individuals carrying PTEN mutations frequently develop megalencephaly, an unusually enlarged brain, alongside elevated rates of autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and brain tumors, a constellation of symptoms known clinically as PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome.

Now, in a study published in Science Advances, the Hippenmeyer group at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), collaborating with researchers at Sorbonne Université in Paris, Yale School of Medicine, and Vetmeduni Vienna, has traced the exact single-cell chain reaction unleashed when Pten is lost in developing brain stem cells.

Because switching off Pten across the entire brain causes severe early lethality in animal models, isolating how the mutation alters individual stem cell behavior has historically been difficult.

Industry observers note that to overcome this hurdle, first author Dr. Osvaldo Miranda Romero, a postdoctoral researcher in Simon Hippenmeyer’s laboratory at ISTA, utilized Mosaic Analysis with Double Markers (MADM), a high-precision genetic lineage-tracing technique that deletes Pten in only a tiny, sparse fraction of cortical radial glial stem cells while tagging them and all their descendants with bright fluorescent markers.

“Until now, we lacked basic information about what Pten mutations mean at the level of individual cells and how they affect cellular output, in other words, the quantity and identity of cells produced from stem cells,” explained Romero.

Tracking these fluorescent cellular family trees across mouse brain development revealed a twofold driver of brain overgrowth:.

To uncover how Pten loss forces stem cells to overproduce astrocytes, the team investigated the intracellular signaling pathways governing glial differentiation. Under typical developmental conditions, radial glial progenitors depend on the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway to transition into astrocytes.

According to recent reports, however, when Romero and colleagues simultaneously switched off both Pten and Egfr in individual radial glial cells, astrocyte overproduction continued unabated. Molecular analysis revealed that Pten-deficient progenitors had completely bypassed the standard EGFR route, rerouting glial differentiation through an alternative signaling cascade: the MAPK pathway.

“Under normal conditions, EGFR is an notable driver of glial-cell formation, whereas MAPK can serve as a kind of alternative route under exceptional circumstances,” Romero noted.

In a recent development, beyond illuminating the developmental origins of autism and megalencephaly, this signaling detour carries direct implications for neuro-oncology. Patients with PTEN mutations face a heightened risk of developing gliomas, aggressive brain tumors composed of astrocytes and other glial cells.

Industry observers note that clinicians frequently treat gliomas with drugs designed to block EGFR signaling, yet many patients eventually develop treatment resistance. By demonstrating that Pten loss allows glial cells to sidestep EGFR via MAPK activation, the study highlights a promising therapeutic target.

“Our findings suggest that the MAPK signaling pathway could be investigated as a potential therapeutic target in such cases in the future,” Romero concluded.

How does losing the Pten gene lead to an unusually large brain (megalencephaly)?

Recent findings suggest that researchers at ISTA found that when individual brain stem cells (radial glia) lack the Pten gene, they lose their natural growth brake, producing about 25% more neurons and significantly more astrocytes than normal. Both the neurons and astrocytes also grow abnormally large, expanding overall brain tissue volume.

What conditions are linked to PTEN mutations in humans?

Mutations in PTEN are associated with PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome, which increases the likelihood of megalencephaly (enlarged brain size), autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and glial brain tumors called gliomas.

How could this discovery help treat brain tumors in the future?

Sources indicate that glial brain tumors are often treated with drugs that block the EGFR signaling pathway, but tumors frequently become resistant. Researchers discovered that cells missing Pten bypass EGFR by switching to the alternative MAPK pathway to make astrocytes—suggesting that targeting MAPK could help overcome drug resistance.

Pten Regulates Neurogenic Radial Glia Lineage Progression and Tunes Neocortical Astrocyte Production in Mapk1/3-dependent Pathway.

According to recent reports, the cerebral cortex consists of immense numbers of diverse cell types derived from radial glial progenitor (RGP) cells. How RGPs generate appropriate quantities of distinct cell types to safeguard a brain of correct size is not well understood. However, genetic aberrations in human, including mutations in PTEN, lead to cortical malformation such as macrocephaly, albeit with unknown etiology.

It has been revealed that here, we used mosaic analysis with double markers (MADM)–based clonal analysis and single-cell phenotyping to decipher the role of Pten in RGP lineage progression during cortical ontogeny. Although neurogenic RGP lineage progression was altered and projection neuron production doubled in the absence of Pten, cortical astrogenesis was drastically increased. Through epistasis experiments, we show that the loss of Pten uncouples astrogenesis from essential growth factor signaling hubs, funneling into MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase).

Collectively, our results suggest that Pten regulates RGP lineage progression with distinct sequential functions in corticogenesis to safeguard the emergence of a correctly sized cortex.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain.
  • Recent findings suggest that adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain.
  • At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain. Using MRI scans of teenagers aged 16 to 19, researchers found that heavy smart-device usage is associated with reduced grey matter volume in memory-related medial temporal regions alongside altered maturation patterns in frontal and visual cortices.

Source: University of Eastern Finland.

Recent findings suggest that adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain. Throughout the late teenage years, neural circuits undergo a natural fine-tuning process known as synaptic pruning—trimming away redundant connections to streamline communication, boost processing efficiency, and sharpen executive control.

At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.

In a neuroimaging investigation conducted at the University of Eastern Finland and Kuopio University Hospital, researchers examined how these everyday lifestyle factors correspond to physical differences in adolescent brain structure.

Led by Doctoral Researcher Hannamari Skog of the Institute of Biomedicine, the study evaluated 44 healthy adolescents aged 16 to 19 (25 girls and 19 boys) drawn from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children (PANIC) study and the FitBrain cohort.

Using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify regional grey matter volume alongside validated lifestyle questionnaires and physical fitness testing (including 50-meter shuttle runs and standing long jumps), the researchers uncovered distinct anatomical patterns tied to digital media habits:.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” explained Skog.

However, Skog noted that larger grey matter volume in visual and executive regions during late adolescence is not necessarily advantageous. Because typical teenage brain maturation involves a healthy reduction in grey matter as neural circuits specialize and become more efficient, persistent volume increases in frontal and occipital areas could signal either intensive visual-motor stimulation from apps and games or a developmental delay in cortical pruning.

Recent findings suggest that “The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog noted. “During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency. The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”.

Movement and cardiovascular-muscular fitness were also reflected across multiple cortical and subcortical regions:.

Because the study relied on a cross-sectional snapshot of 44 adolescents, the authors emphasize that causal relationships and long-term cognitive outcomes require longitudinal follow-up across adulthood.

In a recent development, “The results provide latest information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog concluded. “However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”.

How does heavy screen time affect the teenage brain’s structure?

MRI scans from the University of Eastern Finland show that adolescents with high leisure screen time have smaller grey matter volumes in the medial temporal lobe (critical for memory and learning), alongside larger grey matter volumes in frontal and visual regions, which may reflect either heavy visual-motor gaming demands or a delay in normal adolescent brain pruning.

Why can larger grey matter volume in teenagers sometimes indicate delayed brain development?

During healthy adolescence, the brain naturally trims away excess grey matter through synaptic pruning to become faster and more efficient. Having unusually large grey matter volumes in frontal decision-making areas during late adolescence can therefore indicate that this natural maturational streamlining is running behind schedule.

How did physical activity and fitness affect brain volume in this study?

Higher overall physical activity was linked to larger volume in the right visual (occipital) cortex, while better physical fitness scores were associated with larger parietal lobe volume (involved in attention and spatial perception) and smaller volumes in the hippocampus and posterior cingulate gyrus.

Associations of screen time, physical activity and neuromuscular fitness with brain structure in adolescents.

To explore the associations of total screen time, smart device use, physical activity, and neuromuscular fitness with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

Brain gray matter volumes were assessed using magnetic resonance imaging in 44 healthy adolescents (25 females and 19 males) aged 16–19 years. Physical activity and sedentary behavior questionnaires were used to assess screen time, including smart device use, and physical activity, including organized sports in sports clubs. Neuromuscular fitness was assessed using a score combining results of a 50-m shuttle-run test and a standing long jump test.

Screen time and smart device use were negatively associated with medial temporal lobe volumes but positively associated with supplementary motor cortex and dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex volumes. Screen time was also positively related to left cuneus volume. Total physical activity was positively associated with right inferior occipital gyrus volume, but the association did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Neuromuscular fitness was positively associated with parietal lobe volumes but negatively associated with right hippocampus and left posterior cingulate gyrus volumes, but these associations were no longer statistically significant after correction for multiple testing.

In a recent development, longer screen time was related to lower medial temporal lobe volumes and larger frontal lobe volumes, whereas higher physical activity and better neuromuscular fitness were associated with larger volumes in the parietal and occipital regions. These findings highlight the complex relationships of screen time and physical activity with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

Tech Report: Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you.
  • Industry observers note that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

Industry observers note that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

Work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

Subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

It has been revealed that frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an important open question.

Sources indicate that to study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

In a recent development, this finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

In a recent development, can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

This result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

According to recent reports, such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an important and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

Industry observers note that an area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

We now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

It has been revealed that can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

In a recent development, future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

Industry observers note that finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are at the moment conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

While we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

Brain’s Insula Shapes Pain, Emotion, and the Placebo Effect

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay.
  • Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).
  • Sources indicate that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay. Drawing on 15 years of direct intracranial brain recordings across 87 epilepsy patients, the researchers uncovered a hierarchical network explaining how emotions and expectations actively reshape physical pain.

Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).

Sources indicate that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs. Serving as the primary meeting point where raw physiological signals from the body converge with emotion and conscious thought, the insula shapes everything from acute physical pain and temperature sensation to visceral anxiety and self-awareness.

Yet because of its deep anatomical location, mapping precisely where these distinct functions reside—and how they communicate—has long remained a major challenge in human neuroscience.

Recent findings suggest that now, in a landmark study titled “Functional architecture of the human insula,” an international team led by Dr. Julian Quabs and Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) and Forschungszentrum Jülich (FZJ), working alongside collaborators at Stanford University and the National Research Council (CNR) in Parma, has created the first comprehensive functional atlas of the human insula.

To peer directly into the living human insula, the team analyzed intracranial electrophysiological data collected over roughly 15 years at Stanford University Medical Center from 87 patients undergoing diagnostic monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy.

With patient consent, temporarily implanted depth electrodes allowed investigators to deliver targeted electrical stimulation across the insula while recording real-time sensations, neural activity, and directional connectivity with surrounding cortical networks.

This rare dataset revealed that the human insula is organized into four distinct, cooperating functional zones:.

Crucially, connectivity analyses revealed a powerful directional hierarchy: the cognitive insular pole exerts far stronger downward influence over the sensory rear regions than the sensory zones exert back onto the pole.

Recent findings suggest that “Our findings show that the insula is more than a relay station for bodily signals. It appears to actively shape how we experience pain and our own bodies,” explained lead author Dr. Julian Quabs, who conducted much of the investigation during a research fellowship at Stanford University.

Industry observers note that “This points to a possible neural mechanism through which emotions and expectations can alter how we perceive pain and other physical sensations,” added senior author Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers, Director of the Institute of Anatomy I at HHU and head of the Connectivity group at INM-1, FZJ.

By showing how top-down cognitive signals from the frontal lobe and insular pole directly modulate posterior pain-processing regions, the latest atlas offers a concrete biological circuit underlying phenomena such as the placebo effect—providing a precise anatomical roadmap for future neuromodulation and chronic pain therapies.

What is the insular cortex (insula), and what does it do?

The insula is a region of cerebral cortex folded deep inside the brain that integrates physical signals from the body—such as pain, temperature, and heartbeat, with emotions and conscious awareness, shaping how we perceive both physical sensations and ourselves.

What are the four functional regions discovered in the new insula atlas?

Researchers divided the human insula into four cooperating zones: an upper rear region with a body-part map for pain and temperature; a lower region for widespread bodily sensations; a middle front region linked to chest/abdominal sensations and anxiety; and the front tip (insular pole), which connects to the frontal lobe to direct attention.

How does this study help explain the placebo effect?

The researchers discovered that the cognitive front tip of the insula (the insular pole) communicates strongly with the frontal lobe and sends powerful top-down signals to the pain-sensing regions at the back of the insula, showing how beliefs, expectations, and emotions can actively dial down physical pain.

Functional architecture of the human insula.

The insular cortex has a central role in pain, interoception and feelings, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood.

Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode.

Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception.

Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that why do some fresh skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice?
  • It has been revealed that learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body.
  • The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that why do some fresh skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.

It has been revealed that learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping latest skills persist.

The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.

The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.

Industry observers note that earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The newly introduced study suggests there may be another key mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.

According to recent reports, to investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.

The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice.

In a recent development, the researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.

According to recent reports, on following days, mice that received VNS revealed stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.

"The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," claims Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change.".

Rhythmic Changes in Brain Blood Volume.

The team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.

Sources indicate that using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.

Those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally revealed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.

According to recent reports, "Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," says lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent.".

Exploring the Brain-Body Connection.

Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.

By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.

Breaking: Blocking Gut Cannabinoid Receptors Restores Memory in Fragile X

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers demonstrated that selectively blocking peripheral cannabinoid receptors outside the brain improves memory, synaptic plasticity, and gut barrier integrity in fragile X syndrome mouse models.
  • Source: Pompeu Fabra University / Translational Psychiatry.
  • Fragile X syndrome is the most common single-gene cause of inherited intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers demonstrated that selectively blocking peripheral cannabinoid receptors outside the brain improves memory, synaptic plasticity, and gut barrier integrity in fragile X syndrome mouse models. Tthe study highlights that a one-week treatment restores beneficial gut bacteria and reverses hippocampal cognitive deficits without triggering central nervous system side effects.

Source: Pompeu Fabra University / Translational Psychiatry.

Fragile X syndrome is the most common single-gene cause of inherited intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. Alongside cognitive impairment, memory deficits, hyperactivity, and autistic behaviors, individuals living with the condition frequently experience chronic gastrointestinal dysfunction, highlighting the intricate biological link between gut health and neurodevelopment. Despite decades of research, no targeted pharmacological therapies currently exist to treat the cognitive symptoms of fragile X syndrome.

Now, a study led by the Cognition Biology Research Group at Pompeu Fabra University (UPF) in Barcelona and published in Translational Psychiatry reveals that selectively targeting cannabinoid receptors outside the brain can simultaneously heal the gut microenvironment and rescue cognitive function.

Led by principal investigator Dr. Andrés Ozaita alongside co-first authors Lucía de los Reyes Ramírez and Araceli Bergadà-Martínez, the research demonstrates that just one week of peripheral endocannabinoid inhibition reverses synaptic alterations in the hippocampus and restores intestinal barrier integrity in fragile X mouse models.

The endocannabinoid system, particularly type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors, plays a critical role in regulating synaptic transmission, neuroplasticity, and metabolism. Although CB1 receptors are roughly ten times more concentrated in the brain than in peripheral organs, drugs that broadly block central CB1 receptors often carry unacceptable psychiatric and neurological side effects.

To sidestep central nervous system risks, Ozaita and colleagues tested an experimental compound engineered to act strictly on peripheral CB1 receptors without crossing the blood-brain barrier.

Recent findings suggest that “Unlike other drugs that act on the brain, the compound we have tested acts only on peripheral type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors,” explained Ozaita, director of the Cognition Biology Research Group at UPF. “In the same way as in treatments that act on the brain, in mice with the fragile X mutation, this peripheral treatment enhances memory and increases plasticity, which improves the quality of neuronal connections in the hippocampus.”.

“Seeing that the results are comparable to those obtained using drugs that act on the whole body, we think that the main effect of broad-spectrum drugs is closely linked to their peripheral action,” Ozaita noted.

Because neurodevelopmental conditions frequently co-occur with gastrointestinal disturbances, the team examined how peripheral CB1 blockade influenced the gut microbiome and intestinal lining of fragile X mice.

Baseline analysis revealed pronounced gut dysbiosis and mucosal vulnerability in untreated fragile X mice:.

Following the one-week peripheral CB1 inhibitor regimen, both microbial balance and mucosal defenses rebounded.

Recent findings suggest that “Peripheral pharmacological treatment helps restore the microbiome of mutated mice and increases the expression of the Muc2 gene. These two actions improve the ecosystem and the barrier of the large intestine,” said co-first author Lucía de los Reyes Ramírez.

“We cannot state that this recovery of the intestinal environment is due to the specific inhibition of the CB1 receptors in the intestine, but we can say that peripheral inhibition has a positive effect on the microbiota-gut-brain axis in mice carrying the fragile X mutation,” added co-first author Araceli Bergadà-Martínez.

By showing that cognitive rescue does not require drugs to directly penetrate the brain, and instead can be achieved by modulating the microbiota–gut–brain axis, the findings open a promising translational pathway for fragile X syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders.

Future studies will focus on pinpointing the exact signaling messengers linking peripheral CB1 inhibition to hippocampal synaptic remodeling, laying the groundwork for safer, targeted clinical trials in humans.

How can a drug that doesn’t enter the brain improve memory in fragile X syndrome?

Researchers at Pompeu Fabra University found that blocking peripheral type 1 cannabinoid (CB1) receptors outside the brain improves gut microbiome health and strengthens the intestinal barrier. These positive changes along the microbiota–gut–brain axis translate into healthier neuronal connections and improved memory in the brain’s hippocampus, without causing psychiatric side effects.

What gut abnormalities were found in fragile X syndrome models?

Mice with the fragile X mutation had lower levels of beneficial gut bacteria (Lactobacillus and Akkermansia) and reduced expression of the Muc2 gene, which produces the protective mucus barrier lining the large intestine.

Why is this discovery crucial for developing human treatments?

In a recent development, presently, there is no approved medication to treat intellectual disability or memory impairment in fragile X syndrome, and drugs that block cannabinoid receptors inside the brain often cause adverse neurological side effects. Targeting peripheral receptors outside the brain offers a potentially much safer therapeutic strategy.

A serotonergic mechanism is involved in the pro-cognitive effect of AM6545 treatment in a mouse model of fragile X syndrome.

Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the principal monogenic syndrome leading to inherited intellectual disability and autism. It is caused by the silencing of FMR1 gene that leads to the loss in the expression of its encoded protein, the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMRP). In synapses, FMRP has a key role in local mRNA modulation to maintain synaptic plasticity.

Industry observers note that the Fmr1 KO (FX) mouse model shows cognitive impairment and some of the synaptic traits present in individuals with FXS, together with alterations in gut microbiota. Previous studies revealed that pharmacological and genetic cannabinoid type-1 receptor (CB1R) inhibition significantly prevented central key alterations in FX mice. Here, we aimed to evaluate the effect of a sub-chronic treatment with the largely peripherally-restricted CB1R antagonist AM6545.

We found that AM6545 reduced memory deficits and restored enhanced hippocampal mGluR5-dependent long-term depression and aberrant dendritic spine density in FX mice. At the peripheral level, AM6545 modified altered FX mice fecal microbiota composition and intestinal Muc2 expression, while in the hippocampus AM6545 treatment upregulated hippocampal Htr4, the gene encoding for serotonin receptor 4 (5-HT4R). This upregulation, also observed in cecum, positively correlated with memory performance. Notably, acute pharmacological blockade of 5-HT4R abolished AM6545 pro-cognitive effect.

Sources indicate that our results suggest that repeated peripheral CB1R inhibition ameliorates key central and peripheral alterations in FXS mouse model and modifies the expression of serotonergic receptors important for cognitive performance. Together, this evidence points to the peripheral targeting of CB1R as an approach to alleviate cognitive dysfunction in the FXS context.

#34501. What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions.
  • In a recent development, to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine.
  • Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.

In a recent development, to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.

Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.

When the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an key role in producing the anxious response.

"The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty rapidly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," remarked study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

Industry observers note that the study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.

Tracking the Brain During a Threat.

According to recent reports, patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.

At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.

Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments demonstrated that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.

"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.

Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter.

Industry observers note that cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.

It has been revealed that previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.

"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel said.

The researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel noted the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.

"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.

In a recent development, other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.

The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.

How Young People Are Researching Issues That Matter to Them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • In a recent development, middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

In a recent development, middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

Many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

It has been revealed that research is one important way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate issues, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

In schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

Industry observers note that systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

Industry observers note that relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this problem further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

Recent findings suggest that student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect new students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

Recent findings suggest that our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

Second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the complications that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Recent findings suggest that facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action looks and recommendations.

In a recent development, finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or glitch. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these issues, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

According to recent reports, YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

Further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an problem or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action looks and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

In a recent development, throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions looks and recommendations to address their selected problem.

In a recent development, A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

You can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson aims and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here. IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson plans and other resources.

Recent findings suggest that YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here.

IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

The YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

Power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

The results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action looks.

One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether new routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

In our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

There is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and Latest Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

In a recent development, students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists may have found a new way to reduce harmful inflammation in the brain by targeting a receptor that can already be blocked with existing drugs.
  • Sources indicate that the research, published in Brain and led by Professor Nicholas Barnes at the University of Birmingham, identifies the P2X7 receptor as an key driver of neuroinflammation.
  • In a recent development, the findings could eventually have implications for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions in which inflammation is thought to play a role.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists may have found a new way to reduce harmful inflammation in the brain by targeting a receptor that can already be blocked with existing drugs.

Sources indicate that the research, published in Brain and led by Professor Nicholas Barnes at the University of Birmingham, identifies the P2X7 receptor as an key driver of neuroinflammation. When researchers blocked this receptor, inflammation in human brain tissue was significantly reduced.

In a recent development, the findings could eventually have implications for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions in which inflammation is thought to play a role. These include traumatic brain injury (TBI), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and psychosis.

Blocking a Key Driver of Brain Inflammation.

To investigate the receptor, the researchers used live cultures of human brain cells along with slices of brain tissue collected during neurosurgery. They focused on the P2X7 receptor, which helps trigger inflammatory signaling.

Industry observers note that the team found that P2X7 receptors promote the release of cytokines, proteins that help regulate inflammatory responses. When the researchers used a specific antagonist to block the receptor, the inflammatory response in human brain tissue dropped significantly.

Professor Nicholas Barnes from the College of Medicine and Health at the University of Birmingham and corresponding author of the paper said: "This exciting discovery marks a major step toward repurposing existing therapeutics to combat neuroinflammation at its source. The identification of this receptor could have far-reaching implications for some of the most debilitating and widespread brain disorders such as Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's and Multiple Sclerosis, or inflammation-linked psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and depression.".

Studying the Brain's Immune Cells.

A major part of the work involved microglia, immune cells that help coordinate the brain's response to injury and inflammation.

In a recent development, to study how these cells react to inflammatory signals, the researchers developed a method for converting a type of white blood cell into microglia. This process mirrors a cellular transformation that has recently been identified as occurring naturally in the brain during human aging.

In a recent development, the team started with human peripheral monocytes collected from blood samples and converted them into microglia-like cells. These cells provided a way to examine how human microglia may respond to inflammatory signals.

When the researchers applied the P2X7 receptor antagonist, they were able to interfere with signals released by microglia as the cells became damaged and died.

It has been revealed that professor Barnes mentioned: "Studying human microglia has long been a major challenge: once removed from their native brain environment, they rapidly lose their defining characteristics, likely due to the absence of critical regulatory signals. Our approach involved the use of monocyte-derived microglia which provide a powerful, scalable, and virtually unlimited platform for studying human microglial biology with unprecedented precision.".

From Lab Models to Human Brain Tissue.

After identifying the response in the lab grown microglia-like cells, the researchers tested whether the same findings could be reproduced in human brain tissue obtained through neurosurgical procedures.

The successful results in human tissue strengthen the case for further investigation and could eventually lead to clinical trials in people with neurodegenerative diseases or traumatic brain injury.

Industry observers note that professor Barnes mentioned: "Having identified the response in the human monocyte-derived microglia, this provided the impetus to translate these findings with human brain obtained following neurosurgical procedures. This successful translation means the next stage for this research is the development of clinical trials in patients with neurodegenerative conditions and patients with TBI where there are no effective pharmacological treatments to reduce the neuroinflammation and arising damage.".

  • Recent findings suggest that while some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

Recent findings suggest that while some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

Industry observers note that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four fresh practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

In a recent development, let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

Sources indicate that years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She mentioned, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

Industry observers note that while this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

Sources indicate that this practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

According to recent reports, as managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

According to recent reports, one study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

Sources indicate that the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an key part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

In their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

Sources indicate that we encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health

📅 10 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States.
  • Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.
  • Researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States. According to a 2023 report, about half of U.S. adults experience loneliness, while nearly as many are socially isolated. Despite health consequences that can rival other major risk factors, both problems remain relatively overlooked as urgent public health concerns.

Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.

Loneliness Linked to Fewer Healthy Years.

Researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll. Their first-of-its-kind observational study, published in Nature Communications, found that loneliness and social isolation were associated with the loss of nearly six years of life free from mental disorders such as depression and anxiety. The effects on physical health were smaller, but still significant.

Industry observers note that "Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy," noted lead author Lu Qi, HCA Regents Distinguished Chair and professor in Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine at Tulane. "This includes both physical and mental disease.".

It has been revealed that although loneliness and social isolation are often treated as the same thing in everyday conversation, researchers distinguish between them. Social isolation refers to an objective lack of social connections. Loneliness, by contrast, describes a person's subjective dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationships, regardless of how many social interactions they actually have.

"The findings weren't surprising to me," Qi stated. "Previous studies found that social isolation and loneliness are related to mortality, especially premature mortality, and this study provides additional evidence.".

Tracking More Than 277,000 Adults.

The researchers analyzed data from 277,489 adults between the ages of 40 and 69. At the beginning of the study, none had seven major chronic conditions: diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, dementia, cancer, depression and anxiety.

Using age 50 as a reference point, the team calculated how loneliness and social isolation were associated with the number of years participants could expect to live without these diseases.

It has been revealed that compared with people who experienced neither loneliness nor social isolation, women experiencing both had 2.4 fewer years free from physical disease. Men experiencing both had 1.7 fewer years.

According to recent reports, the difference was even larger for mental health. Women experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived about 3.7 fewer years without mental disorders, while men lived approximately 5.8 fewer years free from those conditions.

Industry observers note that "This comes down to the gender differences between men and women," Qi remarked. "Our research found men are more susceptible to being affected by loneliness. We also know that women tend to live longer than men. There are gender advantages with certain diseases.".

Healthy Habits Help With Isolation, but Not Loneliness.

The researchers also examined whether lifestyle could alter these associations. Healthier habits, including better diet, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and not smoking, measurably reduced the loss of disease-free years associated with social isolation.

In a recent development, loneliness produced a different pattern. A healthier lifestyle did not significantly reduce the additional health risks linked to feeling lonely. That distinction suggests loneliness and social isolation may require different approaches when it comes to protecting health.

The research team plans to study additional population groups in the future and use clinical trials to investigate whether loneliness and social isolation directly cause the health effects observed in the study.

Sports: MLB Brand Identity by Mother Design
